blocks.p: Up to now you have worked in SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS), where you typed SQL and ran it yourself. In this chapter you open Visual Studio 2019 for the first time and write C#, the language your program is written in. The program will run your stored procedures for you, the same ones you wrote in chapter 4.

box.title: What a C# program is made of
box.text: A C# program is a set of files, each ending in .cs. Each file holds a class: a named box of code that does one job. Inside a class are methods: named chunks of code that run when something calls them, the way a stored procedure runs when something executes it. Visual Studio 2019 keeps all the files together in a project, and the project is what you build and run.

words: Project
The set of files that make one program. Visual Studio 2019 builds and runs the whole project at once.
Solution Explorer
The panel on the right of Visual Studio 2019 that lists every folder and file in your project.
Class
A named box of code in a .cs file that does one job, such as talking to the database or holding who is signed in.
Method
A named chunk of code inside a class. Code elsewhere calls it by name, and it runs. Methods are the C# version of stored procedures.
Namespace
The family name of a class, written at the top of its file. Classes in different folders have different family names, such as BikeShop.Data and BikeShop.Forms.
Connection string
One line of text that tells the program where SQL Server is, which database to open and how to sign in to it.
Reference
A ready-made set of code from Microsoft that your project is allowed to use. Most are there from the start, and one has to be added by hand.
Form
A window. Each form is a class with a designer, where you drag buttons and boxes on, and a code tab, where you write what the buttons do.
Control
One thing on a form: a button, a text box, a label. Each control has a Name that the code uses.
Event
Something that happens to a control, such as a click. The code that runs when it happens is an event method, and the designer makes it for you.
Build
Turning your .cs files into a program that can run. Press F6. It either says Build succeeded or lists the errors.
Static
A class marked static has one copy of everything, shared by the whole program, so you never make a new one. Db and Session are static.

stages.title: Tell the program where the database is

screens.title: Read what a connection string is.

blocks.p: In SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) you connected to the server once, by picking a server name in the Connect window. Your program has to do the same thing every time it runs, and it has nobody to pick a name for it. So it reads one line of text that says where the server is, which database to open and how to sign in. That line is the connection string.

The connection string does not live in C# code. It lives in a small settings file called App.config, which Visual Studio 2019 made for you when it made the project. A settings file can be changed without touching any code, which matters when the program moves from the school server to your own machine at home.

rule.text: The connection string is written once, in App.config, and read by one class, Db. No other file in the program ever mentions the server name.

code.title: App.config: the whole file
parts: The first line says that this file is written in XML. The startup part names the version of .NET Framework the program runs on, 4.7.2, which is the version you picked when you made the project. If you had to pick a different number in stage 1, change 4.7.2 here to match it.
The name of the connection string

The connectionStrings part can hold several connection strings, each with a name. Yours has one, named BikeShop. The helper class in the next stage asks for a connection string by this name, so the name here and the name in Db.cs must match exactly.

Three settings, separated by semicolons. Server= names the SQL Server to talk to: (localdb)\mssqllocaldb is the small server inside the Programming Environment, the same name you pick in the Connect window of SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS). Database= names the database to open, BikeShop. Integrated Security=True means sign in as the person who is running the program, so no password is stored in this file.
The provider and the closing tags

The provider is the set of code that knows how to talk to SQL Server, called System.Data.SqlClient. The last two lines close the connectionStrings part and the file. Every tag that opens is closed again, which is how XML works.
code.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8" ?>
<configuration>
  <startup>
    <supportedRuntime version="v4.0" sku=".NETFramework,Version=v4.7.2" />
  </startup>
  <connectionStrings>
    <!-- School: LocalDB inside the Programming Environment.
         At home, change Server= to your own SQL Server name. -->
    <add name="BikeShop"
         connectionString="Server=(localdb)\mssqllocaldb;Database=BikeShop;
           Integrated Security=True;"
         providerName="System.Data.SqlClient" />
  </connectionStrings>
</configuration>

stages.title: The one helper the whole program talks through

screens.title: Read what the helper class does.

blocks.p: In Visual Studio 2019 you now add the most important file in the program: Db.cs. Db is one class that every other class goes through to reach the database. Nothing else in the program opens a connection or names a stored procedure. When a screen needs rows, it asks Db. When a screen needs to change data, it asks Db. That is the rule of this program: every table is touched through a stored procedure, and in C# every stored procedure is run through Db.

Db has four methods. P makes a parameter, which is one value to send to a stored procedure, such as a username. Out makes an output parameter, a slot the stored procedure fills in and the program reads afterwards, such as the new ID of a row that was just added. GetTable runs a stored procedure that selects rows and hands back a table. Run runs a stored procedure that changes data and hands back its message: an empty message means it worked.

rule.text: Every stored procedure is run through Db.GetTable or Db.Run. No form and no other class ever opens its own connection to SQL Server.

screens.title: Read Db.cs: the using lines and the connection string.

blocks.p: The whole file is below. It is long, so it is read in pieces, one region at a time. A region is a named fold in the code, marked with #region at its top and #endregion at its bottom. Visual Studio 2019 can fold a region shut with the small minus sign beside it, so that a long file reads like a list of names.

code.title: Data/Db.cs: the whole file
parts: Each using line names a set of ready-made code this file needs. System.Data.SqlClient is the one that knows how to talk to SQL Server. System.Configuration is the one that reads App.config, and it works because of the reference you added in stage 2.

The namespace line gives the class its family name: this class is BikeShop.Data.Db. The class is static, which means there is one shared copy of it for the whole program, so a form calls Db.GetTable directly without making a Db first. The comment lines above it are the four things to know, in one sentence each.

This is a property, a named value with code behind it. When code asks for ConnectionString, the get part runs: it asks ConfigurationManager for every connection string in App.config, picks the one named BikeShop, and hands back its text. It is private, so only Db can read it, which keeps the server name in one place.

P takes a name, such as @Username, and a value, and wraps them as a SqlParameter, which is what SQL Server expects to receive. The if part handles an empty value: C# calls an empty value null, and SQL Server calls it NULL, and they are not the same thing, so null is swapped for DBNull.Value before it is sent.
Out: a slot the procedure fills in

Out makes a parameter that goes the other way. The stored procedure writes a whole number into it, such as the ID of the row it just added, and the program reads parameter.Value afterwards. Direction set to Output is what tells SQL Server that this one is for writing into.
GetTable: run a procedure that selects rows

GetTable takes the name of a stored procedure and any number of parameters, which is what params means. It makes an empty DataTable, then opens a connection using the connection string and makes a command that names the stored procedure. A using line with a block after it means close this when the block ends, so the connection is always closed, even if something goes wrong. CommandType set to StoredProcedure tells SQL Server that the name is a stored procedure and not a query to read.
GetTable: fill the table and hand it back

A SqlDataAdapter is the piece that runs the command and copies every row it selects into the table. Fill does that in one go. The table is then handed back, and whoever asked can put it straight into a grid on a form.
Run: a procedure that changes data

Run is for stored procedures that insert, update or delete. Every one of those in chapter 4 has an @Message output parameter, so Run makes that parameter itself, 200 characters long, before it starts. The comment above says the rule: an empty message means it worked, and anything else is a sentence to show the user.

The same connection and command as GetTable, with the message parameter added to the list. Open opens the connection, and ExecuteNonQuery runs the stored procedure without expecting rows back. Both using lines close again when the block ends.
Run: when SQL Server itself says no

try and catch mean: try this, and if SQL Server throws an error, run the catch part instead of crashing. A CHECK rule or a foreign key that refuses a change arrives here as a SqlException, and its message is handed back the same way as a message from the stored procedure. So a form only ever sees a sentence, and it never needs try and catch of its own round a database call. The last line hands back whatever the stored procedure put into @Message.

box.title: Why one helper
box.text: If every form opened its own connection, a change to the server name would mean a change on every form, and one form would be bound to get it wrong. With Db, the connection string is read in one place, the closing of connections happens in one place, and the rule about messages is kept in one place. The examiner can see all of it on one page.

StaffMember describes one member of staff: it is a class with six properties and no methods, one for each column of the Staff table except IsActive. Session remembers who is signed in, for the whole program, from sign-in to sign-out. StaffData is the class that asks Db to run the Staff stored procedures. Msg shows message boxes, so that every form says things the same way.

The main menu is a partial class called frmMain, inside the namespace BikeShop.Forms. Like frmLogin, it has a method with the same name as the class that runs when the window is made, and InitializeComponent builds the controls you dragged on.
Load: say who is signed in

This is the Load event method the designer made, so it runs once when the window opens. It builds a sentence out of pieces: the words Signed in, the full name from Session, and the role in brackets. The plus signs join text together. The sentence goes into the label under the title.
// Only a manager sees the money.
Load: switch Reports off for a non-manager

Enabled is whether a button can be pressed. It is set to Session.IsManager, which is true for a manager and false for everyone else, so the button is greyed out for a counter worker or a mechanic. The exclamation mark means not: if the person is not a manager, the text of the button changes to say why it is off. The button stays visible, so everyone knows the reports exist.

When Customers is clicked, a new frmCustomers window is made and shown with ShowDialog. ShowDialog means the main menu waits, and cannot be clicked, until that window is closed again. In C#, the word this means the main menu itself, and passing it in puts the new window in front of the menu.

box.title: Make it yours
box.text: In your own project, the sign-in table is whatever your scenario calls its staff, and the roles are whatever your scenario needs: a manager and a receptionist, or an owner and a groomer. Keep the shape exactly: one stored procedure that checks the username, the password and an active flag; one Session class that remembers who is signed in; and one button on the main menu that only one role can press. Db.cs and Msg.cs do not change at all, and App.config changes only the database name.
